title: Resource-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection for Large-Scale Molecular Diversity Optimization
authors: Nicolas Mendes de Araujo, Lester de Abreu Faria
abstract: Large-scale combinatorial optimization remains demanding for classical heuristics, particularly when dense Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulations induce large memory footprints, high CPU utilization, and long execution times. While near-term quantum processors cannot yet deliver unconditional quantum advantage, hybrid architectures can provide practical value by reducing the resource burden. This paper presents a resource-efficiency study of Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection (HQNS), a framework that decomposes large dense QUBO instances into bounded-width quantum subproblems via stochastic frontier selection. We evaluate HQNS on the Maximum Diversity Subset Selection Problem (MDSSP), focusing on the trade-off between solution quality retention and resource consumption. Benchmarks up to N=1000 candidates show that HQNS preserves 99.9908% of the mean diversity score of an 11-restart parallel Simulated Annealing baseline, while reducing wall-clock time by 94.91%, peak CPU utilization by 64.68%, and peak memory usage by 88.61%. The QPU execution time remains bounded within a 6-7 second envelope across scales, indicating that the quantum component is decoupled from the global QUBO dimension when the frontier size is fixed. These results suggest that HQNS provides a resource-aware pathway for deploying hybrid quantum optimization in practical large-scale settings, serving as an efficient architecture for incorporating near-term quantum processors into classical optimization pipelines.
summary: This paper introduces Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection (HQNS) to tackle large combinatorial optimization problems formulated as dense QUBOs. By decomposing the problem into small, manageable quantum subproblems via frontier selection, HQNS significantly reduces computational resource demands compared to classical methods. This demonstrates a practical, resource-aware pathway for utilizing near-term quantum hardware in complex scientific simulations.
main_problem: Solving large-scale combinatorial optimization problems, specifically those formulated as dense QUBO instances like Maximum Diversity Subset Selection.
main_result: The proposed HQNS framework achieves near-baseline solution quality while drastically reducing computational resource consumption (time, CPU, memory) compared to strong classical baselines on large problem sizes ($N=1000$).
method: HQNS decomposes the large QUBO instance into smaller, bounded-width quantum subproblems by selecting a stochastic 'frontier' of active variables for local optimization on the QPU.
model_or_system: The problem is modeled using QUBO formulations derived from pairwise similarity matrices. The context is Near-Term Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) processors, which struggle with monolithic encoding of large interactions.
key_observables: Diversity score retention (99.9908% vs baseline), wall-clock time reduction (94.91%), peak CPU utilization reduction (64.68%), and QPU execution time stability ($\sim 6-7$ seconds).
important_parameters: Problem size $N$ up to 1000; Frontier size $F \ll N$; QUBO formulation complexity.
main_assumptions: The quantum component's workload is bounded by the fixed frontier size ($F$), decoupling it from the global dimension ($N$) for practical NISQ deployment.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the computational bottleneck of large QUBO problems, introduces HQNS as a resource-aware hybrid solution, evaluates its performance against state-of-the-art classical solvers (SA), and concludes by demonstrating its practical utility for NISQ hardware.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, resource-efficient architectural blueprint for integrating quantum processors into complex optimization pipelines, which is highly relevant for developing algorithms applicable to molecular simulation or material design using near-term hardware.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. Statistical diversity comparison at N = 1000 over ten independent runs. Error bars indicate one standard deviation. SA Parallel-11 achieves the higher mean diversity score, while HQNS preserves 99.9908% of the SA mean diversity.

FIGURE 2. Quality-retention and resource-efficiency summary at N = 1000. HQNS preserves 99.9908% of the SA Parallel-11 mean diversity score while reducing wall-clock time, peak CPU utilization, and peak memory usage.

FIGURE 4. Pareto Analysis of Solution Quality versus Computational Cost at N = 1000. The horizontal axis reports wall-clock execution time, while the vertical axis reports mean diversity score over ten independent runs. Bubble area is proportional to peak memory usage. HQNS occupies an intermediate operational region: it is substantially faster than SA Single and SA Parallel-11, while preserving near-baseline diversity relative to the strongest parallel classical baseline.

FIGURE 3. QPU execution-time stability across problem scales. HQNS maintains a bounded QPU execution envelope because each quantum stage operates on a compact active frontier rather than the full N-variable QUBO.
